s1.title: Square of a Sum
s1.about: Expansion of the square of a sum of two terms. Used to expand brackets quickly and in many proofs.
s1.symbols:
a = first term
b = second term

s10.title: Product Law of Indices
s10.about: When the same base is multiplied, the powers add. Basic rule for all index (exponent) questions.
s10.symbols:
a = the base (same in both)
m, n = the powers (exponents)

s100.about: Derivative of inverse tan — answer is the neat fraction 1/(1 + x^2).
s100.symbols:
tan^-1 = inverse tan (arctan)
x = any real number

s106.about: The power rule for integration — the reverse of differentiation. Increase the power by 1 and divide by the new power. Not valid for n = -1.
s106.example: Integral of x^2 dx = x^3/3 + C. Check by differentiating: d/dx (x^3/3) = x^2.
s106.symbols:
x = the variable
n = the power (n is not -1)
C = constant of integration (never forget it)

s108.about: e^x integrates to itself, plus the constant.
s108.example: Integral of e^(3x) dx = e^(3x)/3 + C (divide by the inner coefficient 3).
s108.symbols:
e = Euler's number, about 2.718
C = constant of integration

s110.about: Integral of sin x is MINUS cos x. The negative sign is the commonest mistake.
s110.symbols:
x = the angle, in radians
C = constant of integration

s111.about: Integral of cos x is sin x — a clean, positive answer.
s111.example: Integral of cos(5x) dx = sin(5x)/5 + C.
s111.symbols:
x = the angle, in radians
C = constant of integration

s116.about: Integral of tan x — a standard result worth memorising: log of sec x.
s116.example: Integral of tan x dx = ln|sec x| + C = -ln|cos x| + C (both forms are the same).
s116.symbols:
sec x = 1 / cos x
C = constant of integration

s128.about: Standard integral of the square root of (a^2 - x^2) — appears in area-of-circle type problems.
s128.example: Integral of √(9 - x^2) dx: here a = 3, so the answer is (x/2)√(9 - x^2) + (9/2) sin^-1(x/3) + C.
s128.symbols:
a = a positive constant
x = the variable
C = constant of integration

s132.about: The most famous standard limit — the base of all derivative-of-sin proofs. x MUST be in radians.
s132.example: lim (sin 3x)/x as x -> 0: rewrite as 3 x (sin 3x)/(3x) = 3 x 1 = 3.
s132.symbols: x = a small angle in RADIANS approaching 0

s140.about: Determinant of a 2x2 matrix — cross-multiply and subtract. The base for inverse, area and system-solving formulas.
s140.symbols: a, b, c, d = the four entries of the matrix (a top-left, d bottom-right)

s144.about: Inverse of a matrix — the matrix equivalent of 1/A. Exists only when the determinant is not zero.
s144.symbols:
A = the square matrix
adj(A) = adjoint (transpose of the cofactor matrix)
|A| = determinant of A (must not be 0)

s162.about: Sum of all eigenvalues of a matrix = sum of its diagonal entries (the trace). A one-line answer in exams.
s162.example: A = [2 1; 1 2]: trace = 2 + 2 = 4. Its eigenvalues are 3 and 1 — and 3 + 1 = 4.
s162.symbols:
lambda = an eigenvalue
trace(A) = sum of the main diagonal entries

s163.about: Product of all eigenvalues of a matrix = its determinant.
s163.example: A = [2 1; 1 2]: |A| = 4 - 1 = 3. Its eigenvalues are 3 and 1 — and 3 x 1 = 3.
s163.symbols:
lambda = an eigenvalue
|A| = determinant of A

s17.about: THE quadratic formula — it gives both roots (solutions) of any quadratic equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0 directly, without factorising.
s17.symbols:
a = coefficient of x^2 (a is not 0)
b = coefficient of x
c = constant term
x = the unknown (the roots are the answers)
D = b^2 - 4ac is the discriminant

s171.about: Taylor series — writes a function as an infinite polynomial around a nearby point a. Used for approximations and limits.
s171.example: For e^x around a = 0 this becomes the Maclaurin series 1 + x + x^2/2! + ...
s171.symbols:
f = the function
f', f'' = its first and second derivatives
a = the point around which the series is built

s172.about: Maclaurin series — the Taylor series around a = 0. Most standard expansions (e^x, sin x, cos x) are Maclaurin series.
s172.example: sin x = x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - ... (put x = 0 in all derivatives of sin).
s172.symbols: f(0), f'(0), ... = the function and its derivatives at x = 0

s173.about: Standard expansion of e^x — works for every x. Memorise the pattern: powers of x divided by factorials.
s173.symbols:
x = any real number
n! = factorial (1 x 2 x ... x n)

s178.about: Standard expansion of ln(1 + x) — alternating signs, valid for -1 < x up to 1.
s178.symbols: x = the small number inside the log (-1 < x <= 1)

s18.about: Shortcut relations between the coefficients and the two roots — no need to solve the equation. Very common in exams.
s18.example: For x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0: sum of roots = -b/a = 5, product = c/a = 6. Indeed the roots are 2 and 3 (2 + 3 = 5, 2 x 3 = 6).
s18.symbols:
alpha, beta = the two roots
a = coefficient of x^2
b = coefficient of x
c = constant term

s198.about: Euler's theorem — for a homogeneous function, this combination of partial derivatives gives back n times the function. A guaranteed exam question in M1.
s198.example: f = x^2 + xy + y^2 (degree 2). x f_x + y f_y = x(2x + y) + y(x + 2y) = 2(x^2 + xy + y^2) = 2f. Matches n f with n = 2.
s198.symbols:
f = a homogeneous function of x and y
n = its degree (total power of each term)
f_x, f_y = partial derivatives w.r.t. x and y

s20.about: Log of a product becomes the sum of logs. Used to break big log expressions into simple parts.
s20.symbols: m, n = the two numbers being multiplied (both positive)

s201.about: Total derivative — how z changes when BOTH x and y change with a third variable t (chain rule for two variables).
s201.example: z = x^2 + y^2 with x = t, y = t^2: dz/dt = 2x(1) + 2y(2t) = 2t + 4t^3. Direct check: z = t^2 + t^4 gives the same 2t + 4t^3.
s201.symbols:
z = function of x and y
x, y = themselves functions of t

s205.about: Jacobian — the determinant of all partial derivatives of u and v. Used when changing variables in double integrals.
s205.example: u = x + y, v = x - y: J = (1)(-1) - (1)(1) = -2, and |J| = 2 is used in the integral.
s205.symbols:
u, v = new variables (functions of x and y)
J = the Jacobian determinant

s208.about: Gamma function — the continuous version of the factorial, defined by this integral. The starting point of all Gamma questions.
s208.example: Gamma(1) = 1 and Gamma(n + 1) = n Gamma(n), so Gamma(4) = 3! = 6.
s208.symbols:
Gamma(n) = gamma of n
n = a positive number
e^-x x^(n-1) = the function being integrated from 0 to infinity

s211.about: The most quoted Gamma value: Gamma of one-half is root pi. Memorise it — it is asked directly.

s219.about: Beta function — an integral of x and (1 - x) powers between 0 and 1, closely linked to the Gamma function.
s219.symbols:
B(m, n) = beta function of m and n
m, n = positive numbers

s22.about: Log of a power — the power comes down in front. Makes log of squares, cubes, roots easy.
s22.symbols:
m = the number (positive)
n = the power

s221.about: Beta-Gamma relation — converts a Beta value into Gamma values, which are easy to compute. The working formula for almost every Beta question.
s221.symbols:
B = beta function
Gamma = gamma function
m, n = the two arguments

s225.about: Reduction formula — lowers the power of sin step by step until it becomes easy. The heart of Wallis' formula questions.
s225.symbols:
I_n = the integral of sin^n x from 0 to pi/2
n = the power (2 or more)

s229.about: King's property — replace x by (a - x) inside a definite integral; the value stays the same. Adding the two forms often makes a hard integral trivial.
s229.example: I = integral of sinx/(sinx + cosx) from 0 to pi/2. By King's property, 2I = integral of 1 dx = pi/2, so I = pi/4.
s229.symbols:
a = the upper limit (lower limit is 0)
f = the function being integrated

s238.about: Area by double integration — the area of a region R is the double integral of 1 over it.
s238.example: Area of the rectangle 0<=x<=2, 0<=y<=3: double integral of dy dx = 2 x 3 = 6.
s238.symbols:
R = the region in the xy-plane
dA = dx dy (small area piece)

s243.about: Volume by triple integration — the volume of a solid is the triple integral of 1 over it.
s243.example: Box 2 x 3 x 4: volume = triple integral of dx dy dz = 24.
s243.symbols: dV = dx dy dz (small volume piece)

s248.about: Variable separable — the simplest differential equation type: push all y terms with dy on one side, all x terms with dx on the other, then integrate both sides.
s248.example: dy/dx = x y. Separate: dy/y = x dx. Integrate: ln y = x^2/2 + C, so y = A e^(x^2/2).
s248.symbols:
dy/dx = derivative of y w.r.t. x
C = constant of integration

s252.about: Linear differential equation — the standard first-order form and its solution using the Integrating Factor (IF). The most important method in Unit 4.
s252.example: dy/dx + y = e^x. P = 1, so IF = e^x. Then y e^x = integral of e^(2x) dx = e^(2x)/2 + C, giving y = e^x/2 + C e^(-x).
s252.symbols:
P, Q = functions of x only
IF = integrating factor = e^(integral of P dx)
C = constant of integration
Method: y x IF = integral of (Q x IF) dx + C

s254.about: Bernoulli's equation — looks non-linear because of the y^n term, but one substitution (v = y^(1-n)) turns it into a linear equation.
s254.example: dy/dx + y = x y^2 (n = 2): divide by y^2 and put v = y^(-1). It becomes a linear equation in v, solved with an IF.
s254.symbols:
P, Q = functions of x
n = the power of y on the right side
v = the substitution y^(1-n)

s255.about: Auxiliary equation — for a higher-order equation with constant coefficients, replace D by m. Its roots decide the whole shape of the solution.
s255.example: y'' - 3y' + 2y = 0 becomes m^2 - 3m + 2 = 0, with roots m = 1, 2.
s255.symbols:
D = d/dx (the differential operator)
m = the unknown whose values are the roots

s256.about: Complementary Function (CF) when the auxiliary equation has two DIFFERENT real roots — each root gives one exponential term.
s256.example: Roots 1 and 2 give y = C1 e^x + C2 e^(2x).
s256.symbols:
m1, m2 = the two distinct real roots
C1, C2 = arbitrary constants

s261.about: Particular Integral rule 1 — for e^(ax) on the right side, simply put D = a in f(D) and divide. Works when f(a) is not zero.
s261.symbols:
f(D) = the operator polynomial on the left side
a = the power in e^(ax)

s269.title: Complex Number — Standard Form
s269.about: The standard form of a complex number — a real part plus an imaginary part. The base of all Unit 5 work.
s269.symbols:
z = the complex number
x = real part Re(z)
y = imaginary part Im(z) — note: the part is y itself, not iy
i = √-1, so i^2 = -1

s27.about: Change of base — converts a log of any base into a base your calculator knows (base 10 or e).
s27.symbols:
a = old base
b = new base (usually 10)
m = the number

s270.about: Modulus of a complex number — its distance from the origin on the Argand diagram. Always a non-negative real number.
s270.symbols:
|z| = modulus of z
x = real part
y = imaginary part

s277.about: Euler's formula — connects the exponential function with cos and sin. Called the most beautiful formula in mathematics when theta = pi.
s277.example: e^(i pi/2) = cos 90 + i sin 90 = i. And e^(i pi) = -1.
s277.symbols:
e = Euler's number
i = √-1
theta = the angle, in radians

s278.about: De Moivre's theorem — raising a complex number (in polar form) to a power: just multiply the angle by the power.
s278.example: (cos30 + i sin30)^3 = cos90 + i sin90 = i.
s278.symbols:
theta = the angle (argument) of the complex number
n = the power (any real number)

s280.about: Cauchy-Riemann equations — the test for whether a complex function is analytic (differentiable). If these fail, the function is not analytic.
s280.example: For f(z) = z^2: u = x^2 - y^2, v = 2xy. u_x = 2x = v_y and u_y = -2y = -v_x — C-R hold everywhere, so z^2 is analytic everywhere.
s280.symbols:
u = real part of f(z)
v = imaginary part of f(z)
u_x etc. = partial derivatives of u and v

s289.about: Cauchy's Integral Formula — the value of an analytic function at a point from an integral around it. The central formula of complex integration.
s289.example: ∮ e^z / z dz (circle around 0) = 2πi x f(0) with f(z) = e^z, so the answer is 2πi x 1 = 2πi.
s289.symbols:
f(a) = value of the function at the point a inside the closed curve
The symbol ∮ means integral around a closed curve (counterclockwise)

s29.about: n-th term of an Arithmetic Progression (AP) — a sequence where the same difference is added every step.
s29.symbols:
a = first term
d = common difference
n = term number
a_n = the n-th term

s3.title: Difference of Two Squares
s3.about: Difference of two squares, factorised. Used for fast factorisation and rationalising.
s3.symbols:
a = first term
b = second term

s31.about: n-th term of a Geometric Progression (GP) — a sequence where every step is multiplied by the same ratio.
s31.symbols:
a = first term
r = common ratio
n = term number

s33.about: Sum of an infinite GP — only works when the ratio is between -1 and 1 (|r| < 1), so terms keep shrinking.
s33.symbols:
a = first term
r = common ratio (|r| < 1)

s37.about: General term of the binomial expansion — finds any single term of (a + b)^n without expanding everything.
s37.symbols:
n = the power
r = term position (term number = r + 1)
C(n, r) = n! / (r! (n - r)!)
a, b = the two terms inside the bracket

s41.about: The most fundamental identity in trigonometry — it connects sin and cos of the same angle. Used in almost every trig proof.
s41.example: If sin(theta) = 3/5, then cos^2(theta) = 1 - 9/25 = 16/25, so cos(theta) = 4/5 (the 3-4-5 triangle).

s6.title: Sum of Two Cubes
s6.symbols:
a = first term
b = second term

s60.about: The bridge between radians and degrees: a half turn (pi radians) is 180 degrees.
s60.example: pi/3 radians = 180/3 = 60 degrees. And 90 degrees = pi/2 radians.

s63.about: Arc length of a circle — the length of a piece of the circumference cut by an angle. The angle MUST be in radians.
s63.example: r = 7 cm, theta = 2 rad: l = 7 x 2 = 14 cm.
s63.symbols:
l = arc length
r = radius of the circle
theta = angle at the centre, in RADIANS

s64.about: sin of a sum or difference of two angles, expanded into sin and cos of the separate angles.

s65.about: cos of a sum or difference of two angles. Note the sign flips: cos(A + B) uses MINUS.
s65.example: cos 75 = cos(45 + 30) = cos45 cos30 - sin45 sin30 = 0.259.

s67.about: Double-angle formula for sin — converts sin of twice an angle into sin and cos of the single angle.

s68.about: Double-angle formula for cos — three useful forms; pick the one that matches your question (all-cos, all-sin, or mixed).

s75.about: Product-to-sum conversion — turns a product of sin and cos into a sum, which is easier to integrate or simplify.

s84.about: The power rule — the single most used derivative rule. Bring the power down and reduce it by 1.
s84.symbols:
x = the variable
n = the power (any real number)

s88.about: e^x is its own derivative — it never changes on differentiation. One of the most special formulas in calculus.
s88.example: d/dx (e^x) = e^x. With the chain rule: d/dx (e^(2x)) = 2e^(2x).
s88.symbols:
e = Euler's number, about 2.718
x = the variable

s90.about: Derivative of the natural log — gives the simple answer 1/x.
s90.example: At x = 2, the slope of ln x is 1/2. And d/dx ln(5x) = 1/x (chain rule).
s90.symbols:
ln = natural log (base e)
x = the variable (x > 0)

s92.about: Derivative of sin x is cos x. (x must be in radians.)
s92.example: d/dx sin(3x) = 3 cos(3x) (chain rule — multiply by the derivative of 3x).

s93.about: Derivative of cos x is MINUS sin x — do not forget the negative sign.

s94.about: Derivative of tan x is sec squared x.
s94.example: d/dx tan x = sec^2 x = 1 + tan^2 x.
s94.symbols:
x = the angle, in radians
sec x = 1 / cos x

s98.about: Derivative of inverse sin — used in integration-by-recognition and inverse-trig questions.
s98.symbols:
sin^-1 = inverse sin (arcsin), NOT 1/sin
x must lie between -1 and 1

s2.title: Square of a Difference
s2.about: Expansion of the square of a difference of two terms. Used to expand brackets quickly and in many proofs.
s2.symbols:
a = first term
b = second term

s4.title: Cube of a Sum
s4.about: Expansion of the cube of a sum. Useful in algebra simplification and in binomial-type questions.
s4.symbols:
a = first term
b = second term

s5.title: Cube of a Difference
s5.about: Expansion of the cube of a difference of two terms.
s5.symbols:
a = first term
b = second term

s7.title: Difference of Two Cubes
s7.about: Factorisation of the difference of two cubes — the reverse of expanding (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2).
s7.symbols:
a = first term
b = second term

s8.title: Square of a Sum of Three Terms
s8.about: Expansion of the square of a sum of three terms — each term squared, plus twice every pair product.
s8.symbols: a, b, c = the three terms

s9.title: Product of (x + a) and (x + b)
s9.about: Shortcut for multiplying two brackets that share the same x term — used in factorising quadratics in reverse.
s9.symbols:
x = variable
a, b = constants in the two brackets

s11.title: Quotient Law of Indices
s11.about: Quotient law of indices: dividing two powers of the same base subtracts the exponents.

s12.title: Power of a Power Law
s12.about: Power of a power law: raising a power to another power multiplies the exponents.

s13.title: Zero Index Law (a⁰ = 1)
s13.about: Zero index law: any non-zero number raised to the power 0 equals 1.
s13.example: 7^0 = 1. This comes from the quotient law: 7^3 / 7^3 = 7^(3-3) = 7^0 = 1.

s14.title: Negative Index Law
s14.about: Negative index law: a negative power means the reciprocal of the positive power.

s15.title: Fractional Index Law (Roots)
s15.about: Fractional index law: a power of 1/n is the same as the n-th root.

s16.title: Power of a Product Law
s16.about: Power of a product law: a power applied to a product applies to every factor inside.

s148.title: Inverse of a Product (AB)⁻¹
s148.about: Inverse of a product: the order REVERSES — (AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}. Like socks and shoes: undo the last one first.
s148.symbols: A, B = invertible matrices of the same size
s148.example: Reason: (AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1}) = A(BB^{-1})A^{-1} = A I A^{-1} = I, so B^{-1}A^{-1} really is the inverse of AB.

s149.title: Inverse of an Inverse (A⁻¹)⁻¹
s149.about: Inverting twice returns the original matrix — the inverse of the inverse is the matrix itself.
s149.example: If A^{-1} has rows (3 -1), (0 2), then the inverse of THAT matrix is the original A — no calculation needed, by this rule.

s150.title: Inverse of a Scalar Multiple (kA)⁻¹
s150.about: Inverse of a scalar multiple: the scalar comes out as its reciprocal. Pulling k out of an n x n determinant gives k^n, but the inverse only takes one 1/k — a common confusion point.
s150.symbols:
k = non-zero scalar
A = invertible matrix

s151.title: Inverse of a Transpose (Aᵀ)⁻¹
s151.about: Inverse and transpose commute: the inverse of the transpose equals the transpose of the inverse, either order gives the same matrix.
s151.example: To find (A^T)^{-1}, either transpose A and then invert, or invert A and then transpose — both give the same answer; pick whichever is easier.

s181.title: Binomial Expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ
s181.about: The binomial expansion for ANY power n (including fractions and negatives) — it never terminates unless n is a positive whole number, and needs |x| < 1 in that case. The first two expansions below are its special cases.
s181.symbols:
n = any real power
x = value with |x| < 1 (for non-integer n)

s182.title: Expansion of (1 − x)⁻¹
s182.about: Expansion of 1/(1 - x) — the geometric series 1 + x + x^2 + ..., valid for |x| < 1. The mother of many other expansions.

s183.title: Expansion of (1 − x)⁻²
s183.about: Expansion of 1/(1 - x)^2 — the coefficients are simply 1, 2, 3, 4, ... It comes from differentiating the (1 - x)^{-1} series.

s204.title: Implicit Function — Total Derivative
s204.about: For an implicit relation f(x, y) = 0, you cannot always solve for y — but dy/dx is still available: minus (partial of f w.r.t. x) over (partial of f w.r.t. y), treating f as a function of two variables.
s204.symbols:
f = the implicit relation set to zero
∂f/∂x = partial derivative with y treated constant

s239.title: Volume under a Surface
s239.about: Volume under a surface: the double integral of the height function over the base region. Set up limits from the region's boundaries, integrate inside-out.
s239.symbols:
V = volume
f(x, y) = height of the surface above (x, y)
R = base region
s239.example: Volume under z = 1 - x - y over the triangle x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x + y ≤ 1: ∫ from 0 to 1 ∫ from 0 to 1-x (1 - x - y) dy dx = 1/6.

s19.about: The discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac tells the nature of the roots of a quadratic before solving: D > 0 two distinct real roots, D = 0 two equal roots, D < 0 no real roots (complex pair).
s19.symbols:
D = discriminant
a, b, c = coefficients of ax^2 + bx + c = 0
s19.example: For x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0: D = 25 - 24 = 1 > 0, so two distinct real roots (they are 2 and 3).

s21.about: Quotient rule of logarithms: the log of a division is the difference of the logs.
s21.symbols:
m, n = positive numbers
Base is the same for all logs

s23.about: The logarithm of 1 is always 0, in every base — because any base to the power 0 is 1.
s23.example: log 1 = 0 and ln 1 = 0, since 10^0 = 1 and e^0 = 1.

s24.about: The logarithm of the base itself is always 1, because base^1 = base.

s25.about: The natural logarithm of e is 1 — ln uses base e, and the log of the base itself is always 1.
s25.example: ln e = 1, and also ln(e^3) = 3 by the power rule.

s26.about: A power and a logarithm with the same base cancel each other — they are inverse operations.
s26.symbols:
a = base (a > 0, a ≠ 1)
m = positive number
s26.example: 10^{log 50} = 50, exactly — the power undoes the log.

s28.about: A logarithm answers the question: 'to what power must the base be raised to get this number?' If a^x = m then x = log of m to base a. 'ln' means log to base e. Logs turn multiplication into addition, which is why they simplify hard calculations.
s28.symbols:
a = base (a > 0, a ≠ 1)
m = the number (m > 0)
x = the logarithm value

s30.about: Sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic progression (AP). The second form (n/2)(a + l) is handy when the last term is known.
s30.symbols:
S_{n} = sum of first n terms
a = first term
d = common difference
l = last (n-th) term

s32.about: Sum of the first n terms of a geometric progression (GP) when the common ratio r > 1 (for r < 1 the mirrored form is used).
s32.symbols:
S_{n} = sum of first n terms
a = first term
r = common ratio (r ≠ 1)

s34.about: Factorial: the product of all whole numbers from n down to 1. Used everywhere in permutations, combinations and series. By definition 0! = 1.
s34.symbols:
n = a non-negative whole number
n! is read 'n factorial'

s35.about: The number of ways to choose r items from n items when the order does not matter (combinations).
s35.symbols:
n = total items
r = items chosen
nCr is read 'n choose r'

s36.about: Symmetry of combinations: choosing r items to take is the same as choosing n - r items to leave out, so the two values are equal. A big calculation shortcut.
s36.symbols:
n = total items
r = items chosen
s36.example: 10C8 = 10C2 = 45 — much easier to compute with 2 than with 8.

s38.about: The basic definitions of the trigonometric ratios in a right-angled triangle: sin = perpendicular/hypotenuse, cos = base/hypotenuse, tan = perpendicular/base. Every other ratio (cosec, sec, cot) is the reciprocal of one of these.
s38.symbols:
θ = the angle being considered
Perpendicular = side opposite to θ
Base = side next to θ (not the hypotenuse)
Hypotenuse = the longest side, opposite the right angle
s38.example: In a 3-4-5 triangle, for the angle opposite the side 3: sin θ = 3/5 = 0.6, cos θ = 4/5 = 0.8, tan θ = 3/4 = 0.75.

s39.about: The standard values of sin, cos, tan and their reciprocals at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90° — these must be memorised; they come in almost every exam.
s39.symbols:
θ = angle
The radian measure is written in brackets
s39.example: sin 60° = √3/2 ≈ 0.866 and cos 30° = √3/2 as well — notice sin and cos swap values between 30° and 60°.

s40.about: A memory trick for the standard sin values: for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° the sin values are √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2. Cos is the same list in reverse order, and tan = sin/cos.
s40.example: sin 45° = √2/2 = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707, read straight off the pattern.

s42.about: Fundamental identity linking tan and sec — divide sin^2θ + cos^2θ = 1 by cos^2θ to get it. Used to simplify expressions and prove identities.
s42.example: If tan θ = 3/4, then sec^2θ = 1 + 9/16 = 25/16, so sec θ = 5/4 (taking θ acute).

s43.about: Fundamental identity linking cot and cosec — divide sin^2θ + cos^2θ = 1 by sin^2θ to get it.
s43.example: If cot θ = 5/12, then cosec^2θ = 1 + 25/144 = 169/144, so cosec θ = 13/12 (θ acute).

s44.about: Sin is an odd function: changing the sign of the angle changes the sign of sin. Useful for negative angles.

s45.about: Cos is an even function: the sign of the angle does not matter for cos. Useful for negative angles.

s46.about: Tan is an odd function: changing the sign of the angle changes the sign of tan.

s47.about: Allied angle rule: sin of (90° - θ) equals cos θ — sin and cos are complementary, which is exactly why it is called 'co-sine'.
s47.example: sin 60° = cos 30° = √3/2 — both sides say the same thing with θ = 30°.

s48.about: Allied angle rule: cos of (90° - θ) equals sin θ.
s48.example: cos 75° = sin 15° — handy when only one of the pair is known.

s49.about: Allied angle rule: tan of (90° - θ) equals cot θ.
s49.example: tan 80° = cot 10°, and since cot 10° = 1/tan 10°, tan 80° is large while tan 10° is small.

s50.about: Allied angle rule for just past 90°: sin(90° + θ) is still cos θ (sin stays positive in the second quadrant).

s51.about: Allied angle rule: cos(90° + θ) = -sin θ — cos becomes negative in the second quadrant.

s52.about: Allied angle rule: sin(180° - θ) = sin θ — sin is positive throughout the second quadrant.

s53.about: Allied angle rule: cos(180° - θ) = -cos θ — cos flips sign in the second quadrant.

s54.about: Allied angle rule: sin(180° + θ) = -sin θ — sin becomes negative in the third quadrant.

s55.about: Allied angle rule: cos(180° + θ) = -cos θ — cos is also negative in the third quadrant.

s56.about: Allied angle rule: tan(180° + θ) = tan θ — tan is positive in the third quadrant (and repeats every 180°).

s57.about: Allied angle rule: sin(360° - θ) = -sin θ — sin is negative in the fourth quadrant.

s58.about: Allied angle rule: cos(360° - θ) = cos θ — cos stays positive in the fourth quadrant.

s59.about: The ASTC rule tells the sign of ratios in each quadrant: 1st quadrant All positive, 2nd only Sin (and cosec), 3rd only Tan (and cot), 4th only Cos (and sec). Remember it as 'All Silver Tea Cups'.
s59.symbols: θ = angle, measured from the positive x-axis
s59.example: 150° is in the 2nd quadrant: sin 150° is positive (1/2) while cos 150° and tan 150° are negative.

s61.about: One radian in degrees: a radian is the angle whose arc length equals the radius, and it works out to about 57.3 degrees.
s61.symbols:
π ≈ 3.14159
rad = radian, the SI unit of angle

s62.about: One degree in radians — the basic conversion used to turn any degree measure into radians: multiply degrees by π/180.

s66.about: Tan of a sum or difference of two angles, written using the tans of the parts. Note the sign pattern: same sign on top, opposite sign below.

s69.about: Tan of double the angle, from the tan(A + B) formula with A = B.

s70.about: Sin of three times an angle, written using sin of the angle alone.

s71.about: Cos of three times an angle, written using cos of the angle alone. Notice it mirrors the sin 3A pattern.

s72.about: Half-angle formula: sin squared of A/2 in terms of cos A. Used to find values at 15°, 22.5° and in integration.
s72.example: sin^2(30°) with A = 60°: (1 - cos 60°)/2 = (1 - 0.5)/2 = 0.25, so sin 30° = 0.5 (positive, 30° is in the 1st quadrant).

s73.about: Half-angle formula: cos squared of A/2 in terms of cos A.

s74.about: Half-angle formula: tan squared of A/2 as a ratio of (1 - cos A) and (1 + cos A).

s76.about: Product-to-sum conversion: twice cos A sin B written as a difference of two sines. Used to integrate products of trig functions.
s76.example: 2 cos 60° sin 30° = sin 90° - sin 30° = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5. Check directly: 2 x 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.5.

s77.about: Product-to-sum conversion: twice cos A cos B written as a sum of two cosines. Used to integrate products of trig functions.

s78.about: Product-to-sum conversion: twice sin A sin B written as a difference of two cosines. Mind the order — cos(A - B) comes first.

s79.about: Sum-to-product conversion: a sum of two sines becomes a product — half the sum of angles inside sin, half the difference inside cos.

s80.about: Sum-to-product conversion: a difference of two sines becomes a product of cos (half-sum) and sin (half-difference).

s81.about: Sum-to-product conversion: a sum of two cosines becomes a product of two cosines — half-sum and half-difference.

s82.about: Sum-to-product conversion: a difference of two cosines becomes a product of two sines, with a minus sign in front.

s83.about: The derivative dy/dx measures how fast y changes when x changes a little — geometrically it is the slope of the tangent to the curve at that point. Almost every differentiation question is built from the master rule d/dx(x^n) = n x^{n-1} plus the working rules.
s83.symbols:
dy/dx = derivative of y with respect to x
x = independent variable
y = dependent variable (a function of x)
s83.example: For y = x^3, dy/dx = 3x^2. At x = 2 the slope is 3 x 4 = 12 — the curve is rising steeply there.

s85.about: The derivative of any constant is zero — a constant never changes, so its rate of change is 0.
s85.example: d/dx (7) = 0, and in y = x^2 + 5 the +5 disappears on differentiating: dy/dx = 2x.

s86.about: Derivative of root x. Write √x as x^{1/2} and use the power rule — the answer is 1/(2√x).
s86.example: At x = 4: d/dx(√x) = 1/(2 x 2) = 1/4 — the curve y = √x flattens as x grows.

s87.about: Derivative of 1/x. Write 1/x as x^{-1} and use the power rule: the answer is -1/x^2.
s87.example: For y = 1/x at x = 2: dy/dx = -1/4. The negative sign says y decreases as x increases.

s89.about: Derivative of an exponential with any base a — the function reproduces itself, multiplied by ln a. For base e, ln e = 1, giving the famous d/dx(e^x) = e^x.

s91.about: Derivative of log base a of x. For the natural log (a = e) it reduces to 1/x, since ln e = 1.
s91.symbols:
a = base of the logarithm
x = variable (x > 0)

s95.about: Derivative of cot x is -cosec squared x. Remember the minus sign — it comes with cot, cos and cosec derivatives.

s96.about: Derivative of sec x is sec x tan x — sec reproduces itself times tan.
s96.example: At x = 0: sec 0 tan 0 = 1 x 0 = 0 — the sec curve is flat at its minimum point x = 0.

s97.about: Derivative of cosec x is -cosec x cot x, with a minus sign like all 'co' functions.
s97.example: At x = 90° (π/2): -cosec(π/2) cot(π/2) = -1 x 0 = 0 — flat at the minimum of cosec.

s99.about: Derivative of inverse cos — the negative of the inverse sin derivative; the two add to zero because sin^{-1}x + cos^{-1}x is a constant (π/2).

s101.about: Derivative of inverse cot — the negative of the inverse tan derivative.

s102.about: Derivative of inverse sec. The x outside the root is taken positive in the standard (principal) range used in this course.

s103.about: Derivative of inverse cosec — the negative of the inverse sec derivative.

s104.about: The three working rules of differentiation. Product rule for a product u·v, quotient rule for a division u/v, and chain rule for a function inside a function — in the chain rule, differentiate the outer function, keep the inner as it is, then multiply by the derivative of the inner.
s104.symbols:
u, v = functions of x
u' or du/dx = derivative of u
s104.example: Product rule: d/dx (x · e^x) = x·e^x + e^x·1 = e^x(x + 1). Chain rule: d/dx (sin(x^2)) = cos(x^2) · 2x.

s105.about: Integration is differentiation in reverse: finding a function whose derivative is the given function. Every indefinite integral carries a constant + C, because differentiating a constant gives zero so it cannot be recovered. A definite integral (with limits) gives the area under the curve.
s105.symbols:
∫ = integral sign
dx = with respect to x
C = constant of integration
s105.example: ∫ 3x^2 dx = x^3 + C — check by differentiating: d/dx(x^3 + C) = 3x^2. Correct.

s107.about: The integral of 1/x is ln|x| — the one power the power rule cannot handle (n = -1 would divide by zero). The modulus keeps it valid for negative x too.
s107.symbols:
ln = natural logarithm
C = constant of integration
s107.example: ∫ from 1 to e of (1/x) dx = ln e - ln 1 = 1 - 0 = 1.

s109.about: Integral of an exponential with base a — itself divided by ln a (the reverse of its derivative).
s109.symbols:
a = base (a > 0, a ≠ 1)
C = constant of integration
s109.example: ∫ 2^x dx = 2^x / ln 2 + C. Check with the definite integral from 0 to 1: (2 - 1)/ln 2 ≈ 1.44.

s112.about: Integral of sec squared is tan — the reverse of d/dx(tan x) = sec^2 x.
s112.symbols:
x = angle in radians
C = constant of integration
s112.example: ∫ from 0 to π/4 of sec^2 x dx = tan(π/4) - tan 0 = 1 - 0 = 1.

s113.about: Integral of cosec squared is -cot — the reverse of d/dx(cot x) = -cosec^2 x. Note the minus sign in the answer.
s113.symbols:
x = angle in radians
C = constant of integration
s113.example: ∫ from π/4 to π/2 of cosec^2 x dx = [-cot x] = -cot(π/2) + cot(π/4) = 0 + 1 = 1.

s114.about: Integral of sec x tan x is sec x — the reverse of d/dx(sec x).
s114.symbols:
x = angle in radians
C = constant of integration
s114.example: ∫ from 0 to π/3 of sec x tan x dx = sec(π/3) - sec 0 = 2 - 1 = 1.

s115.about: Integral of cosec x cot x is -cosec x — the reverse of d/dx(cosec x), minus sign included.
s115.symbols:
x = angle in radians
C = constant of integration
s115.example: ∫ from π/6 to π/2 of cosec x cot x dx = [-cosec x] = -1 + 2 = 1.

s117.about: Integral of cot x — write it as cos x / sin x; the numerator is the derivative of the denominator, giving ln|sin x|.
s117.symbols:
x = angle in radians
C = constant of integration
s117.example: ∫ from π/6 to π/2 of cot x dx = ln(sin(π/2)) - ln(sin(π/6)) = ln 1 - ln(1/2) = ln 2 ≈ 0.693.

s118.about: Integral of sec x — a standard result worth memorising: ln|sec x + tan x|. (The cosec one has a minus inside instead.)
s118.symbols:
x = angle in radians
C = constant of integration

s119.about: Integral of cosec x — standard result: ln|cosec x - cot x|. Compare with sec, where the sign inside is plus.
s119.symbols:
x = angle in radians
C = constant of integration
s119.example: ∫ from π/4 to π/2 of cosec x dx = ln(1 - 0) - ln(√2 - 1) = -ln(0.414) ≈ 0.881.

s120.about: Integral of sin squared — first rewrite it with the half-angle identity sin^2 x = (1 - cos 2x)/2, then integrate term by term.
s120.symbols:
x = angle in radians
C = constant of integration
s120.example: ∫ from 0 to π of sin^2 x dx = [x/2 - sin 2x/4] from 0 to π = π/2 - 0 = π/2 ≈ 1.571.

s121.about: Integral of cos squared — use cos^2 x = (1 + cos 2x)/2 first. Only the sign of the sin 2x term differs from the sin squared integral.
s121.symbols:
x = angle in radians
C = constant of integration
s121.example: ∫ from 0 to π of cos^2 x dx = π/2 — the same as sin squared over a full half-period, which makes sense since the two curves are shifts of each other.

s122.about: Standard form: integral of 1/(x^2 + a^2) gives (1/a) tan inverse of (x/a). One of the six standard forms to memorise.
s122.symbols:
a = positive constant
C = constant of integration

s123.about: Standard form: integral of 1/√(a^2 - x^2) gives sin inverse of (x/a). Valid for |x| < a.
s123.symbols:
a = positive constant
C = constant of integration

s124.about: Standard form: integral of 1/(a^2 - x^2) gives a log ratio, with 1/(2a) outside. Watch the order: (a + x) over (a - x).
s124.symbols:
a = positive constant
C = constant of integration

s125.about: Standard form: integral of 1/(x^2 - a^2) gives a log ratio with (x - a) over (x + a) — the mirror image of the a^2 - x^2 form (and its answer differs by sign).
s125.symbols:
a = positive constant
C = constant of integration

s126.about: Standard form: integral of 1/√(x^2 + a^2) gives ln|x + √(x^2 + a^2)|. No inverse function appears — it is a log.
s126.symbols:
a = positive constant
C = constant of integration

s127.about: Standard form: integral of 1/√(x^2 - a^2) gives ln|x + √(x^2 - a^2)|. Valid for x > a.
s127.symbols:
a = positive constant
C = constant of integration

s129.about: Standard form: integral of √(x^2 + a^2) — the answer has an x/2 times root part plus an (a^2/2) log part. All three root-integrals follow this same pattern.
s129.symbols:
a = positive constant
C = constant of integration

s130.about: Standard form: integral of √(x^2 - a^2) — same pattern as the +a^2 version but the log term is SUBTRACTED.
s130.symbols:
a = positive constant
C = constant of integration

s131.about: Integration by Parts handles a product: ∫u·v dx = u∫v dx - ∫(u' · ∫v dx) dx; choose u by the ILATE order (Inverse, Log, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential — first in the list becomes u). Partial fractions splits a rational function into simple pieces by writing it as a sum of fractions with linear/quadratic denominators.
s131.symbols:
u = the part to differentiate (chosen by ILATE)
v = the part to integrate
s131.example: ∫ x e^x dx by parts (u = x): x e^x - ∫ e^x dx = e^x(x - 1) + C.

s133.about: Standard limit: tan x / x approaches 1 as x approaches 0 (x in radians). It follows from the famous sin x / x limit.
s133.example: lim of tan(0.01)/0.01 ≈ 1.00003 — already very close to 1 for small x.

s134.about: Standard limit: (e^x - 1)/x approaches 1 as x approaches 0. The basis of the derivative of e^x.

s135.about: Standard limit: (a^x - 1)/x approaches ln a as x approaches 0 — for a = e it gives 1, matching the e^x limit.
s135.example: For a = 2: lim (2^x - 1)/x = ln 2 ≈ 0.693 as x → 0.

s136.about: Standard limit: ln(1 + x)/x approaches 1 as x approaches 0. The basis of the derivative of ln x.

s137.about: Standard limit: (1 + x)^{1/x} approaches e ≈ 2.718 as x approaches 0 — one of the definitions of e. The (1 + 1/n)^n form is the same idea for large n.

s138.about: Standard limit: (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) approaches n·a^(n-1) as x approaches a — this is exactly the power rule for derivatives in disguise.
s138.symbols:
n = any real power
a = the point approached

s139.about: A caution that ties the standard limits together: limits like sin x / x = 1 hold only when x is measured in radians. These limits are the foundation of the series expansions (Taylor and Maclaurin) in Unit 2.
s139.example: sin(0.01 rad)/0.01 ≈ 0.99998 ≈ 1, but with 0.01 degrees the ratio is completely different — always convert to radians first.

s141.about: Expanding a 3x3 determinant along the first row: each element times its cofactor (the 2x2 determinant left after deleting its row and column), with signs + - + across the row.
s141.symbols: a to i = the nine entries of the matrix, row by row

s142.about: The minor of an element is the small determinant left after deleting its row and column; the cofactor is the minor with a sign (-1)^{i+j} — positive on the checkerboard squares where i + j is even. Cofactors build the adjoint and the inverse.
s142.symbols:
M_{ij} = minor of the element in row i, column j
C_{ij} = its cofactor
s142.example: In rows (1 2 3), (0 1 4), (5 6 0), the minor of 2 (row 1, col 2) deletes row 1 and column 2, leaving det of (0 4 / 5 0) = -20; its cofactor is -(-20) = 20 since (-1)^{1+2} = -1.

s143.about: The most-asked determinant properties: swapping two rows flips the sign; identical or proportional rows make it zero; a scalar pulled out of one row multiplies the value (from all rows of an n x n matrix, k comes out as k^n); adding a multiple of one row to another leaves it unchanged; a triangular determinant equals the product of its diagonal.
s143.example: If |A| = 5 for a 3x3 matrix, then |2A| = 2^3 x 5 = 40 — the 2 comes out of all 3 rows.

s145.about: The defining property of the adjoint: A times adj(A) equals |A| times the identity matrix. Dividing by |A| gives the inverse formula A^{-1} = adj(A)/|A|.
s145.symbols:
adj(A) = adjoint (transpose of the cofactor matrix)
|A| = determinant
I = identity matrix
s145.example: For A with rows (2 0), (0 3): adj(A) has rows (3 0), (0 2), and A·adj(A) has rows (6 0), (0 6) = 6I — indeed |A| = 6.

s146.about: The determinant of the inverse is the reciprocal of the determinant — a direct consequence of |AB| = |A||B| applied to A·A^{-1} = I.

s147.about: Determinant of the adjoint: |adj A| = |A|^{n-1} for an n x n matrix. Comes from taking determinants on both sides of A·adj(A) = |A| I.

s152.about: Adjoint of a product also reverses order: adj(AB) = adj(B) adj(A), exactly like the inverse rule.
s152.symbols: A, B = square matrices of the same size
s152.example: This follows from the inverse rule: adj(AB) = |AB|(AB)^{-1} = |A||B| B^{-1}A^{-1} = adj(B) adj(A).

s153.about: A symmetric matrix equals its own transpose — it is a mirror image across the main diagonal, so entry (i, j) equals entry (j, i).
s153.example: The matrix with rows (1 2), (2 5) is symmetric: transposing swaps the two 2s with each other, giving back the same matrix.

s154.about: A skew-symmetric matrix equals the negative of its transpose. Comparing diagonal entries with themselves forces every diagonal entry to be 0.
s154.example: Rows (0 3), (-3 0): the transpose is rows (0 -3), (3 0), which is exactly -A. Note the zeros on the diagonal.

s155.about: An orthogonal matrix has its transpose as its inverse — inverting is free. Such matrices represent rotations and reflections; their determinant is always +1 or -1.
s155.example: The rotation matrix rows (cos θ, -sin θ), (sin θ, cos θ) is orthogonal: multiplying it by its transpose gives I for every θ.

s156.about: An idempotent matrix squares to itself: A^2 = A. Projection matrices are the standard example — projecting twice changes nothing the second time.
s156.example: A = rows (1 0), (0 0) (projection onto the x-axis): A^2 = rows (1 0), (0 0) = A.

s157.about: An involutory matrix is its own inverse: A^2 = I. Reflections are the standard example, and its inverse is itself.
s157.example: A = rows (0 1), (1 0) (swap): A^2 = rows (1 0), (0 1) = I — swapping twice restores the original.

s158.about: Every square matrix splits uniquely into a symmetric part (A + A^T)/2 plus a skew-symmetric part (A - A^T)/2. A standard exam proof question.
s158.example: For A with rows (1 4), (2 3): symmetric part = rows (1 3), (3 3), skew part = rows (0 1), (-1 0); adding them returns A.

s159.about: The rank is the number of independent rows (columns) of a matrix — equivalently the size of its largest non-zero minor. Find it by reducing to echelon form with elementary row operations and counting the non-zero rows. Rank decides consistency of equations and much more.
s159.symbols:
ρ(A) or rank(A) = the rank
Echelon form = staircase form after row operations
s159.example: Rows (1 2), (2 4): the second row is twice the first, so rank = 1 — only one independent row.

s160.about: Consistency test for AX = B by comparing ranks: if rank(A) ≠ rank of the augmented matrix [A|B], no solution; if both equal the number of unknowns n, a unique solution; if both equal some r < n, infinitely many solutions with n - r free variables.
s160.symbols:
A = coefficient matrix
[A | B] = augmented matrix (B attached as a column)
n = number of unknowns
s160.example: x + y = 3 and 2x + 2y = 7: rank(A) = 1 but rank([A|B]) = 2, so no solution — the lines are parallel and never meet.

s161.about: An eigenvalue λ with eigenvector X means the matrix only stretches X: AX = λX, with X non-zero. Eigenvalues come from the characteristic equation |A - λI| = 0; each eigenvalue's eigenvectors come from solving (A - λI)X = 0.
s161.symbols:
λ = eigenvalue (a scalar)
X = eigenvector (non-zero)
I = identity matrix
s161.example: For A with rows (2 0), (0 3): λ = 2 with X = (1, 0), and λ = 3 with X = (0, 1) — a diagonal matrix stretches each axis separately.

s164.about: For a triangular (or diagonal) matrix, the eigenvalues are simply the diagonal entries — because A - λI stays triangular and its determinant is the product of diagonal terms.
s164.example: The upper triangular matrix with rows (1 5 9), (0 4 2), (0 0 -3) has eigenvalues 1, 4 and -3 straight from the diagonal.

s165.about: Inverting a matrix reciprocates its eigenvalues: if λ is an eigenvalue of A, then 1/λ is an eigenvalue of A^{-1}, with the same eigenvector.
s165.example: If A has eigenvalues 2 and 4, then A^{-1} has eigenvalues 1/2 and 1/4.

s166.about: Powers of a matrix raise its eigenvalues to the same power: λ becomes λ^k for A^k, with the same eigenvector. (Apply AX = λX repeatedly.)
s166.symbols:
λ = eigenvalue of A
k = positive whole number power
s166.example: If λ = 3 for A, then A^2 has eigenvalue 9 and A^3 has 27 for the same eigenvector.

s167.about: Adding cI shifts every eigenvalue by c: A + cI has eigenvalues λ + c, with the same eigenvectors.
s167.symbols:
λ = eigenvalue of A
c = scalar
I = identity matrix
s167.example: If A has eigenvalue 5, then A + 2I has eigenvalue 7 for the same eigenvector.

s168.about: Multiplying a matrix by a scalar k multiplies every eigenvalue by k as well.
s168.symbols:
λ = eigenvalue of A
k = scalar
s168.example: If A has eigenvalues 1 and -2, then 3A has eigenvalues 3 and -6.

s169.about: Cayley-Hamilton theorem: every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation — substitute the matrix itself for λ and the result is the zero matrix. Two big uses: computing A^{-1} by rearranging the equation, and reducing high powers of A to lower ones.
s169.symbols: The characteristic equation = |A - λI| = 0 written in λ
s169.example: For A with rows (2 0), (0 3): characteristic equation is λ^2 - 5λ + 6 = 0, and indeed A^2 - 5A + 6I = rows (4 0), (0 9) - rows (10 0), (0 15) + rows (6 0), (0 6) = zero matrix.

s170.about: The Taylor series rewrites a function as an infinite polynomial around a point x = a, using its derivatives at a. Maclaurin series is the same thing at a = 0. This is how calculators find sin, e^x and ln values, and how we approximate quantities like sin 31° or e^{0.1}.
s170.symbols:
f^{n}(a) = n-th derivative of f at x = a
a = the point around which we expand
n! = n factorial

s174.about: Maclaurin expansion of sin x — only odd powers, alternating signs, x in radians. Memorise it.
s174.symbols:
x = angle in radians
n! = n factorial

s175.about: Maclaurin expansion of cos x — only even powers, alternating signs, x in radians. Memorise it.

s176.about: Maclaurin expansion of tan x — only odd powers, but the coefficients are NOT simple factorials (unlike sin and cos).

s177.about: Maclaurin expansion of inverse tan — odd powers divided by the power itself, alternating signs.

s179.about: Expansion of ln(1 - x) — all signs negative, each power divided by itself. It is the ln(1 + x) series with x replaced by -x. Valid for -1 ≤ x < 1.
s179.symbols: x = value in the range -1 ≤ x < 1

s180.about: Expansion of a^x for any base a — it is the e^x series with x replaced by x ln a.
s180.symbols:
a = base (a > 0)
ln a = natural log of a

s184.about: Maclaurin expansion of inverse sin — odd powers with fractional coefficients (1/6, 3/40, ...).
s184.symbols:
x = value with |x| ≤ 1
Answer comes out in radians

s185.about: Expansion of sinh x — exactly like sin x but with ALL signs positive (no alternation).
s185.symbols:
x = any real value
sinh = hyperbolic sine

s186.about: Expansion of cosh x — exactly like cos x but with ALL signs positive.
s186.symbols:
x = any real value
cosh = hyperbolic cosine

s187.about: How expansions are used in exams: to expand in powers of (x - a), either apply the Taylor formula directly with derivatives at a, or substitute t = x - a, expand in t using a standard series, then replace t back. Keep only as many terms as the question asks.
s187.symbols:
a = the point of expansion
t = x - a (the shifted variable)
s187.example: e^x in powers of (x - 1): e^x = e · e^{x-1} = e[1 + (x - 1) + (x - 1)^2/2! + ...] using the standard e^t series.

s188.about: n-th derivative of e^{ax}: every differentiation brings down one factor of a, so after n differentiations we get a^n e^{ax}.
s188.example: For e^{3x}, the 4th derivative is 3^4 e^{3x} = 81 e^{3x}.

s189.about: The n-th derivative of x^n is the constant n! — each differentiation reduces the power by 1 and multiplies by the falling power, ending at n·(n-1)···1.
s189.symbols:
D^n = n-th derivative
n! = n factorial
s189.example: The 4th derivative of x^4 is 4! = 24 — check: x^4 → 4x^3 → 12x^2 → 24x → 24.

s190.about: n-th derivative of sin(ax + b): each differentiation multiplies by a and adds π/2 to the angle. After n steps: a^n sin(ax + b + nπ/2).
s190.symbols:
D^n = n-th derivative
a, b = constants
s190.example: The 2nd derivative of sin(3x): 3^2 sin(3x + π) = -9 sin(3x) — matches direct differentiation.

s191.about: n-th derivative of cos(ax + b) — the same pattern as sin: multiply by a^n and add nπ/2 to the angle.
s191.symbols:
D^n = n-th derivative
a, b = constants
s191.example: The 1st derivative of cos(2x + 1) by the formula: 2 cos(2x + 1 + π/2) = -2 sin(2x + 1). Correct.

s192.about: n-th derivative of (ax + b)^m: the power falls like a factorial pattern m(m-1)...(m-n+1), each step also brings out one factor a, and the power drops to m - n.
s192.symbols:
D^n = n-th derivative
m = the original power
a, b = constants
s192.example: The 2nd derivative of (x + 1)^5 (a = 1, m = 5): 5 x 4 x (x + 1)^3 = 20(x + 1)^3.

s193.about: n-th derivative of 1/(x + a): alternating sign (-1)^n, an n! on top, and the power in the denominator rises to n + 1.

s194.about: n-th derivative of ln(ax + b): alternating sign starting positive, (n-1)! on top, a^n from the chain rule, and (ax + b)^n below.
s194.symbols:
D^n = n-th derivative
a, b = constants
s194.example: The 2nd derivative of ln(x) (a = 1, b = 0): (-1)^{1} (1!) (1) / x^2 = -1/x^2 — matches differentiating 1/x.

s195.about: n-th derivative of e^{ax} sin(bx + c): the pair (a, b) behaves like a rotation — amplitude factor (a^2 + b^2)^{n/2} and phase shift nφ where φ = tan^{-1}(b/a). This is the hardest standard n-th derivative; learn the pattern.
s195.symbols:
D^n = n-th derivative
φ = tan^{-1}(b/a), the phase angle
s195.example: For e^x sin x (a = b = 1): φ = π/4, and the 2nd derivative is (2)^{1} e^x sin(x + π/2) = 2 e^x cos x.

s196.about: Leibnitz's theorem gives the n-th derivative of a PRODUCT: it looks like the binomial expansion, with nCr coefficients, where the total order of differentiation across u and v always sums to n. Subscripts show the order: u_{n} means the n-th derivative of u, v (with no subscript) is undifferentiated.
s196.symbols:
u, v = the two functions
u_{k} = k-th derivative of u
^{n}C_{r} = binomial coefficient
s196.example: 2nd derivative of x^2 e^x: take u = e^x (all derivatives e^x), v = x^2: e^x·x^2 + 2·e^x·2x + e^x·2 = e^x(x^2 + 4x + 2).

s197.about: A homogeneous function scales uniformly: replacing (x, y) by (tx, ty) multiplies the value by t^n. Quick test: in every term, the total power of x and y together is the same number n — that n is the degree. Homogeneous functions are exactly what Euler's theorem applies to.
s197.symbols:
n = degree of the function
t = any scaling factor
s197.example: f = x^2 + 3xy + y^2: every term has total power 2, so it is homogeneous of degree 2. Check: f(2x, 2y) = 4x^2 + 12xy + 4y^2 = 4f = 2^2 f. Correct.

s199.about: The second-order form of Euler's theorem — the weighted sum of second partial derivatives equals n(n-1)u. It follows by applying the first-order theorem to the partial derivatives themselves.
s199.symbols:
u = homogeneous function of degree n
∂ = partial derivative symbol

s200.about: Euler's theorem in disguise: when u itself is not homogeneous but F(u) is (for example u = sin^{-1}(...) where the inside is a ratio), first identify what F(u) is — here F(u) would be sin u — state its degree n, then x·u_x + y·u_y = n·F(u)/F'(u).
s200.symbols:
F = the outer function (sin, tan, ln, ...)
F'(u) = its derivative
n = degree of F(u) as a homogeneous function
s200.example: If u = tan^{-1}((x^3 + y^3)/(x - y)), then tan u = (x^3 + y^3)/(x - y) is homogeneous of degree 2, so x·u_x + y·u_y = 2 tan u / sec^2 u = 2 sin u cos u = sin 2u.

s202.about: The total differential dz collects the full small change in z = f(x, y): the x-contribution (∂z/∂x)dx plus the y-contribution (∂z/∂y)dy. It is the basis of error estimation.
s202.symbols:
dz = total small change in z
dx, dy = small changes in x and y
∂z/∂x = partial derivative with y fixed
s202.example: For z = x^2 y at (2, 3): dz = 2xy dx + x^2 dy = 12 dx + 4 dy. If dx = 0.01 and dy = 0.02, dz ≈ 0.12 + 0.08 = 0.20.

s203.about: Approximate error: the error in a computed quantity z is estimated by the total differential, replacing d with Δ (the measurement errors). Worst case: take all terms with positive signs.
s203.symbols:
Δz = approximate error in z
Δx, Δy = errors in measuring x and y

s206.about: The Jacobian J = ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) is the determinant of the partial-derivative matrix. If J = 0 everywhere, u and v are functionally dependent (one is a function of the other); if J ≠ 0, they are independent and (x, y) can be recovered from (u, v). Also J(u,v) · J(x,y) = 1.
s206.symbols:
J = Jacobian determinant
u, v = functions of x and y
s206.example: u = x + y, v = (x + y)^2: v is literally u^2, so they are dependent — and indeed every term of J cancels to 0.

s207.about: Method for maxima and minima of f(x, y): (1) Solve ∂f/∂x = 0 and ∂f/∂y = 0 together for stationary points. (2) At each point compute r = f_{xx}, s = f_{xy}, t = f_{yy}. (3) Decide: rt - s^2 > 0 with r < 0 gives a maximum, with r > 0 a minimum; rt - s^2 < 0 gives a saddle point (neither); rt - s^2 = 0 needs deeper investigation.
s207.symbols: r, s, t = the three second derivatives at the point
s207.example: f = x^2 + y^2: stationary point (0, 0); r = 2, s = 0, t = 2, rt - s^2 = 4 > 0 and r > 0 — a minimum, f = 0. Correct, squares are never negative.

s209.about: The recurrence of the Gamma function: Γ(n + 1) = n·Γ(n). It lets you step any value down towards Γ(1) or Γ(1/2), whose values are known.
s209.symbols:
Γ = Gamma function
n = any positive real number

s210.about: The anchor value Γ(1) = 1 — it agrees with the factorial bridge, since Γ(1) = 0! = 1. Every whole-number value is built by stepping up from here.

s212.about: For whole numbers the Gamma function is just the factorial shifted by one: Γ(n + 1) = n!. This is the bridge between factorials and the Gamma function.

s213.about: A useful half-value: Γ(3/2) = √π/2. It comes from Γ(1/2) = √π by one step of the recurrence.

s214.about: Γ(5/2) = 3√π/4 — two recurrence steps above Γ(1/2). Half-integer values always end as a fraction times √π.

s215.about: Γ(7/2) = 15√π/8 — keep stepping: each half-step multiplies by the previous n (5/2, then 3/2, then 1/2).

s216.about: The reflection formula connects Γ(n) with Γ(1 - n) — it is how values for negative and fractional arguments (like Γ(-1/2)) are found.
s216.symbols: n = any value that is not a whole number

s217.about: Legendre's duplication formula relates Γ at n and n + 1/2 to Γ at 2n — mainly used to prove other results and to evaluate Beta-type integrals quickly.
s217.example: n = 1: Γ(1)·Γ(3/2) = 1 x √π/2 = √π/2; the formula gives (√π/2^{1})·Γ(2) = √π/2. Matches.

s218.about: The Gamma function Γ(n) = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of t^{n-1} e^{-t} dt extends the factorial beyond whole numbers. Whenever an integral has the form ∫ x^{something} e^{-x} or a sin/cos power over 0 to π/2, think Gamma and Beta.
s218.symbols:
Γ(n) = Gamma of n
t = the integration variable
s218.example: ∫ from 0 to ∞ of x^4 e^{-x} dx = Γ(5) = 4! = 24 — no integration by parts needed.

s220.about: The infinite (improper) form of the Beta function, over 0 to ∞. The trigonometric form (0 to π/2) is the one used most in this course.
s220.symbols:
B(m, n) = Beta function
m, n = positive values
s220.example: With the Gamma relation B(m, n) = Γ(m)Γ(n)/Γ(m + n): B(2, 3) = (1! x 2!)/4! = 2/24 = 1/12.

s222.about: The Beta function is symmetric — swapping m and n changes nothing, because the defining integral is symmetric in the two parameters. Often halves the work.
s222.example: B(5, 2) = B(2, 5) — compute whichever order makes the Gamma values easier.

s223.about: The trigonometric form of Beta: integrals of sin and cos powers from 0 to π/2 are Beta functions in disguise — match the powers: sin exponent 2m - 1, cos exponent 2n - 1.
s223.example: ∫ from 0 to π/2 of sin^3 x dx: cos power 0 gives n = 1/2, sin power 3 gives m = 2. B(2, 1/2) = Γ(2)Γ(1/2)/Γ(5/2) = (1 x √π)/(3√π/4) = 4/3; times the leading 1/2 of the trig form... the integral equals (1/2)B(2, 1/2) = 2/3. Correct by direct integration too.

s224.about: The famous shortcut: the integral of sin^m x cos^n x from 0 to π/2 equals Γ((m+1)/2) Γ((n+1)/2) / (2 Γ((m+n+2)/2)). It swallows Wallis' formula and all sin-cos power integrals in one line — memorise it.
s224.symbols:
m = power of sin
n = power of cos
s224.example: ∫ from 0 to π/2 of sin^2 x dx: m = 2, n = 0 gives Γ(3/2)Γ(1/2) / (2Γ(2)) = (√π/2)(√π)/(2 x 1) = π/4. Correct.

s226.about: Wallis' formula for ∫ sin^n x from 0 to π/2 when n is EVEN: a descending fraction of odd numbers over even numbers, times π/2. (Cos^n gives the same values.)
s226.example: ∫ from 0 to π/2 of sin^4 x dx = (3 x 1)/(4 x 2) x π/2 = 3π/16 ≈ 0.589.

s227.about: Wallis' formula when n is ODD: a descending fraction with NO π/2 factor at the end — the missing π/2 is the only difference from the even case, and the most common slip.

s228.about: A famous result worth quoting directly: the integral of ln(sin x) from 0 to π/2 equals -(π/2) ln 2. It is proved using the symmetry property ∫ f = ∫ f(a - x).
s228.example: Numerically: -(π/2)(0.693) ≈ -1.088. The integral is negative because sin x < 1 on the interval, so ln(sin x) < 0.

s230.about: For a symmetric interval -a to a: even functions double the 0-to-a integral; odd functions cancel to zero. Check f(-x) before integrating anything.
s230.symbols:
Even: f(-x) = f(x), like x^2, cos x
Odd: f(-x) = -f(x), like x^3, sin x
s230.example: ∫ from -1 to 1 of x^3 dx = 0 instantly (odd), and ∫ from -π/2 to π/2 of cos x dx = 2 x 1 = 2 (even).

s231.about: The 0 to 2a property: if f(2a - x) = f(x) the integral doubles the 0-to-a part; if f(2a - x) = -f(x) it vanishes. It is the -a to a property shifted.
s231.example: ∫ from 0 to 2π of sin x dx: sin(2π - x) = -sin x, so the integral is 0 — the positive and negative halves cancel.

s232.about: The 'King' property: ∫ from 0 to a of f(x) dx equals ∫ from 0 to a of f(a - x) dx. Adding the two forms often makes impossible-looking integrals trivial — the standard trick for ∫ x sin x / (1 + cos^2 x) type questions.
s232.example: I = ∫ from 0 to π/2 of sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx. By the property, I also equals the cos version; adding: 2I = ∫ 1 dx = π/2, so I = π/4.

s233.about: Swapping the limits of a definite integral flips its sign. Integration from a to b is the negative of integration from b to a.
s233.example: If ∫ from 1 to 4 of f = 10, then ∫ from 4 to 1 of f = -10.

s234.about: An integral with equal limits is zero — there is no interval, so no area accumulates.
s234.example: ∫ from 3 to 3 of (x^5 + sin x) dx = 0, whatever the function is.

s235.about: Splitting intervals: the integral from a to b equals the integral a to c plus c to b, for any c in between (even outside, with care). Essential for modulus and piecewise functions — split at the sign-change points.
s235.example: ∫ from -1 to 2 of |x| dx: split at 0: ∫ from -1 to 0 of (-x) dx + ∫ from 0 to 2 of x dx = 0.5 + 2 = 2.5.

s236.about: The a/2 shortcut: ∫ from 0 to a of f(x)/(f(x) + f(a - x)) dx always equals a/2, whatever f is (as long as the denominator never vanishes). Pure property work — no integration at all.
s236.symbols:
a = upper limit
f = any suitable function
s236.example: ∫ from 0 to π/2 of sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx = (π/2)/2 = π/4 — the same answer the King property gave.

s237.about: A double integral ∬ f(x, y) dA is the volume under the surface z = f(x, y) above the region R; with f = 1 it gives the area of R. Evaluation is iterated: hold one variable, integrate w.r.t. the other, then integrate the result. The limits must describe R carefully — sketch the region first.
s237.symbols:
R = region in the xy-plane
dA = dx dy (area element)
s237.example: ∬ over the unit square of (x + y) dA = ∫ from 0 to 1 [∫ from 0 to 1 (x + y) dy] dx = ∫ from 0 to 1 (x + 1/2) dx = 1.

s240.about: Area between two curves: integrate (top curve minus bottom curve). Find the intersection points first — they usually give the limits a and b.
s240.symbols:
f = upper curve
g = lower curve
a, b = intersection x-values
s240.example: Between y = x and y = x^2 (they meet at 0 and 1; the line is on top): A = ∫ from 0 to 1 (x - x^2) dx = 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6.

s241.about: Changing a double integral to polar coordinates: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, and dx dy becomes r dr dθ. The extra r is the Jacobian — forgetting it is the most common error in this topic. Use polar whenever the region is a circle or the function contains x^2 + y^2.
s241.symbols:
r = distance from origin
θ = angle from the x-axis
s241.example: Area of a circle radius R: ∫ θ from 0 to 2π ∫ r from 0 to R of r dr dθ = 2π x R^2/2 = πR^2. Correct.

s242.about: A triple integral extends the idea to a solid: ∭ f dV with f = 1 gives the volume. Evaluate as three nested single integrals; for spheres and cylinders switch to spherical or cylindrical coordinates.
s242.symbols:
V = the solid region
dV = dx dy dz (volume element)
s242.example: Volume of a box 2 x 3 x 4: ∭ 1 dV = 2 x 3 x 4 = 24 — the triple integral just multiplies the three side lengths.

s244.about: Spherical polar coordinates for triple integrals: best for spheres. The volume element is r^2 sin φ dr dφ dθ — the r^2 sin φ factor is the Jacobian and must not be dropped.
s244.symbols:
r = distance from origin
φ = angle down from the z-axis (0 to π)
θ = angle around the z-axis (0 to 2π)
s244.example: Volume of a sphere radius R: ∫∫∫ r^2 sin φ dr dφ dθ = (R^3/3) x 2 x 2π = (4/3)πR^3. Correct.

s245.about: Cylindrical polar coordinates: polar in the xy-plane, z unchanged. Volume element r dr dθ dz — best for cylinders and paraboloids.
s245.symbols:
r, θ = polar coordinates in the plane
z = height as usual
s245.example: Volume of a cylinder radius R, height h: ∫∫∫ r dr dθ dz = (R^2/2) x 2π x h = πR^2 h. Correct.

s246.about: The area under a curve y = f(x) from a to b is the definite integral of y dx — provided the curve stays above the x-axis; where it dips below, the integral subtracts, so split the range for total geometric area.
s246.symbols:
A = area
a, b = the x-limits
s246.example: Area under y = x^2 from 0 to 2: ∫ x^2 dx = 8/3 ≈ 2.67.

s247.about: Order of a differential equation = the order of its highest derivative; degree = the power of that highest derivative after the equation is made polynomial in the derivatives. The general solution of an n-th order equation contains exactly n arbitrary constants — that count is a quick check on any answer.
s247.symbols:
y' = dy/dx (first derivative)
y'' = second derivative
C = arbitrary constant
s247.example: y'' + 5y' + 6y = 0 has order 2, degree 1, and its solution y = C1 e^{-2x} + C2 e^{-3x} carries exactly 2 constants. Correct.

s249.about: A homogeneous first-order equation: dy/dx depends only on the ratio y/x. Substitute y = vx; then dy/dx = v + x dv/dx, and the equation always becomes separable in v and x. Homogeneous here means every term has the same total degree — check before choosing this method.
s249.symbols: v = the new variable, y = vx
s249.example: dy/dx = (x + y)/x = 1 + y/x. With y = vx: v + x dv/dx = 1 + v, so x dv/dx = 1, v = ln x + C, giving y = x ln x + Cx.

s250.about: An equation M dx + N dy = 0 is exact when ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x — it means M dx + N dy is the total differential of some function, so the solution comes straight from integrating, no integrating factor needed.
s250.symbols:
M = coefficient of dx (a function of x, y)
N = coefficient of dy
s250.example: (2xy + 3) dx + (x^2 + 4y) dy = 0: ∂M/∂y = 2x and ∂N/∂x = 2x — equal, so the equation is exact.

s251.about: Solution of an exact equation: integrate M with respect to x (y held constant), then add the integral of only those terms of N that do NOT contain x, and set the total equal to C. Integrating the full N would double-count.
s251.symbols:
M, N = the coefficients of dx and dy
C = arbitrary constant
s251.example: Continuing (2xy + 3) dx + (x^2 + 4y) dy = 0: ∫M dx = x^2 y + 3x; from N only 4y has no x: ∫4y dy = 2y^2. Solution: x^2 y + 3x + 2y^2 = C.

s253.about: Solving a linear first-order equation dy/dx + P y = Q, step by step: (1) force the coefficient of dy/dx to be exactly 1; (2) read off P and compute the integrating factor IF = e^{∫P dx}; (3) the solution is y·IF = ∫ Q·IF dx + C. If the equation is linear in x instead (dx/dy + P x = Q), swap the roles of x and y.
s253.symbols:
P, Q = functions of x only (after step 1)
IF = integrating factor
s253.example: dy/dx + 2y = e^x: IF = e^{2x}. Then y e^{2x} = ∫ e^{3x} dx + C = e^{3x}/3 + C, so y = e^x/3 + C e^{-2x}.

s257.about: Complementary function when the auxiliary equation has an EQUAL (repeated) root m: the second solution picks up a factor x — y = (C1 + C2 x) e^{mx}. A triple root adds an x^2 term as well.
s257.symbols:
m = the repeated root
C1, C2 = arbitrary constants
s257.example: y'' - 4y' + 4y = 0: auxiliary equation m^2 - 4m + 4 = (m - 2)^2 = 0, root 2 repeated. Solution: y = (C1 + C2 x) e^{2x}.

s258.about: Complementary function for complex roots α ± iβ: the answer is real — e^{αx}(C1 cos βx + C2 sin βx). If the same pair repeats, multiply the bracket by (C3 + C4 x) and add.
s258.symbols:
α = real part of the root
β = imaginary part (β > 0)
s258.example: y'' + 4y = 0: roots ± 2i, so α = 0, β = 2, and y = C1 cos 2x + C2 sin 2x.

s259.about: Purely imaginary roots ± iβ are the complex case with α = 0, so the e^{αx} factor is just 1 and the solution is a pure oscillation C1 cos βx + C2 sin βx — nothing grows or decays.
s259.example: y'' + 9y = 0 gives y = C1 cos 3x + C2 sin 3x — simple harmonic motion.

s260.about: If the auxiliary equation has the root 0 twice (the equation is just y'' = 0 after removing other terms), the complementary function is a straight line: C1 + C2 x.
s260.example: y'' = 0 integrates directly: y' = C2, then y = C1 + C2 x.

s262.about: PI for e^{ax} when the straight rule fails because f(a) = 0 (a is a root of the auxiliary equation): multiply by x and divide by f'(a) instead. If f'(a) is also 0, repeat with x^2/2! and f''(a).
s262.symbols:
f(D) = the operator polynomial
f(a) = it with D replaced by a

s263.about: PI for sin ax or cos ax: if the operator is a function of D^2 only, replace D^2 by -a^2 and simplify. If the denominator becomes 0 (failure), multiply by x and differentiate the operator with respect to D, then proceed.
s263.symbols:
D = d/dx operator
a = the frequency in sin ax / cos ax
s263.example: PI of sin 2x for 1/(D^2 + 4): replace D^2 by -4 → denominator 0 — failure case. Multiply by x and differentiate: PI = x · 1/(2D) sin 2x = -x cos 2x / 4... precisely x/(2D) applied to sin 2x gives -x cos(2x)/4.

s264.about: PI for a polynomial x^m: expand 1/f(D) as a series in ascending powers of D using the binomial expansion, act term by term, and stop — every derivative beyond the m-th is zero on x^m, so the answer terminates.
s264.symbols:
D = d/dx operator
m = degree of the polynomial

s265.about: The shift theorem: for e^{ax} times another function V, pull e^{ax} outside and shift every D inside to (D + a). Then the remaining 1/f(D + a) acts only on V by the other PI rules.
s265.symbols:
V = the function multiplied by e^{ax}
D = d/dx operator
s265.example: PI of e^{2x} sin x for 1/(D^2 + 1): e^{2x} · 1/((D + 2)^2 + 1) sin x = e^{2x} · 1/(D^2 + 4D + 5) sin x; replace D^2 by -1: e^{2x} · 1/(4D + 4) sin x = e^{2x}(sin x - cos x)/8.

s266.about: The Euler-Cauchy equation: x^2 y'' + a x y' + b y = 0 (or with a function on the right). Recognition mark: the power of x in each coefficient exactly matches the order of the derivative it multiplies. It is NOT constant-coefficient until transformed.
s266.example: x^2 y'' + 3x y' + y = 0 is Euler-Cauchy: the x^2 matches y'', the x^1 matches y', and y has x^0.

s267.about: Solving Euler-Cauchy: substitute x = e^z (so z = ln x). Then xD becomes the new operator θ = d/dz, and x^2 D^2 becomes θ(θ - 1). The equation turns into a constant-coefficient equation in z — solve it, then put z = ln x back at the end.
s267.symbols:
θ = d/dz, the operator in z
z = ln x
s267.example: x^2 y'' + 3x y' + y = 0 becomes [θ(θ - 1) + 3θ + 1] y = (θ + 1)^2 y = 0, root -1 repeated: y = (C1 + C2 z) e^{-z} = (C1 + C2 ln x)/x.

s268.about: Powers of i cycle with period 4: i, -1, -i, 1, then repeat. To simplify i^n, divide n by 4 and use the remainder.
s268.example: i^{17}: 17 = 4 x 4 + 1, remainder 1, so i^{17} = i^1 = i. And i^{2026}: remainder 2, so i^{2026} = -1.

s271.about: A complex number times its conjugate gives the squared modulus — a real number. This is how division is done: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom.
s271.symbols:
z = x + iy
z̄ = x - iy (the conjugate)
|z| = √(x^2 + y^2) (the modulus)

s272.about: Modulus of a product is the product of the moduli — lengths multiply when complex numbers multiply (and arguments add).
s272.example: |(1 + i)(√3 + i)| = |1 + i| x |√3 + i| = √2 x 2 = 2√2 ≈ 2.83 — much faster than multiplying out first.

s273.about: Modulus of a quotient is the quotient of the moduli (denominator non-zero).
s273.symbols: z_{1}, z_{2} = two complex numbers, z_{2} ≠ 0

s274.about: The triangle inequality: the modulus of a sum never exceeds the sum of the moduli — geometrically, one side of a triangle is shorter than the other two together. Equality holds when both numbers point in the same direction.

s275.about: The argument is the angle the number makes with the positive x-axis. tan^{-1}(y/x) alone gives the reference angle — always correct it for the quadrant of the point (x, y); the principal value lies in (-π, π].
s275.symbols:
arg z = argument (angle) of z
x = real part
y = imaginary part
s275.example: z = -1 + i is in the 2nd quadrant: reference angle tan^{-1}(1) = π/4, so arg z = π - π/4 = 3π/4. (Using the raw calculator value -π/4 would be wrong.)

s276.about: The polar form writes z using its length r and angle θ instead of x and y: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), also written r e^{iθ}. Multiplication, powers and roots are all easiest in this form.
s276.symbols:
r = |z|, the modulus
θ = arg z, the argument

s279.about: f(z) = u + iv is analytic in a region if it is differentiable at every point there. The working test is the Cauchy-Riemann equations u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x (with continuous partials). Polynomials are analytic everywhere; 1/z is analytic except at 0; z̄, Re z, |z| are analytic nowhere — a favourite exam classification.
s279.symbols:
u = real part of f
v = imaginary part of f
u_x = ∂u/∂x, etc.
s279.example: f(z) = z^2: u = x^2 - y^2, v = 2xy. u_x = 2x = v_y and u_y = -2y = -v_x — C-R holds everywhere, so z^2 is entire (analytic everywhere).

s281.about: The Cauchy-Riemann equations in polar coordinates — needed when u and v are given in terms of r and θ. The 1/r factors are easy to forget; both equations carry exactly one.
s281.symbols:
r, θ = polar coordinates
u, v = real and imaginary parts
s281.example: If u = ln r and v = θ (this is log z): ∂u/∂r = 1/r and (1/r)∂v/∂θ = 1/r — first equation holds; similarly the second. So log z is analytic (away from 0 and the negative x-axis).

s282.about: Once C-R holds, the derivative f'(z) can be computed from ANY of these forms — pick whichever partials are easiest. It also means f'(z) is the same from every direction, the heart of complex differentiability.
s282.symbols:
f'(z) = derivative of f at z
u_x = ∂u/∂x, v_x = ∂v/∂x, etc.
s282.example: For f = z^2 (u = x^2 - y^2, v = 2xy): f'(z) = u_x + i v_x = 2x + i(2y) = 2(x + iy) = 2z. Correct.

s283.about: A function is harmonic if it satisfies Laplace's equation u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0. If f = u + iv is analytic, both u and v are automatically harmonic, and v is called the harmonic conjugate of u — finding it (by integrating the C-R equations, or by Milne-Thomson) is the standard Unit 5 problem.
s283.symbols: u, v = real and imaginary parts of an analytic function
s283.example: u = x^2 - y^2: u_{xx} = 2, u_{yy} = -2, sum = 0 — harmonic. Its conjugate is v = 2xy (+ constant), rebuilding f(z) = z^2.

s284.about: A line (contour) integral ∫ f(z) dz along a curve C: evaluate by parametrising the curve, z = z(t), and converting to an ordinary integral in t — or shortcut with Cauchy's theorems when the curve is closed.
s284.symbols:
C = the path of integration
z(t) = a parametrisation of C
s284.example: ∫ along the straight line from 0 to 1 + i of z dz: parametrise z = (1 + i)t, dz = (1 + i) dt, t from 0 to 1: (1 + i)^2 ∫ t dt = (2i)(1/2) = i.

s285.about: The ML-inequality bounds a line integral: its modulus is at most M (the largest value of |f| on the curve) times L (the length of the curve). Used to show integrals vanish or to estimate them, not to compute exact values.
s285.symbols:
M = maximum of |f(z)| on C
L = length of the curve C
s285.example: |∫ over |z| = 1 of dz/(z^2 + 2)| ≤ M·L: on |z| = 1, |z^2 + 2| ≥ 2 - 1 = 1 so M = 1, L = 2π, giving the bound 2π.

s286.about: Cauchy's integral theorem: if f is analytic in a simply connected region, the integral around EVERY closed curve in it is zero — no singularities inside means nothing accumulates. Most Unit 5 closed integrals are settled by checking analyticity first.
s286.symbols:
∮ = integral around a closed curve
C = the closed curve
s286.example: ∮ over |z| = 1 of z^3 dz = 0, because z^3 is analytic everywhere — no need to parametrise.

s287.about: The one basic non-zero closed integral: ∮ dz/(z - a) = 2πi if the point a lies inside the curve, and 0 if a is outside. Everything in Cauchy's formula family is built on this.
s287.symbols:
a = the centre (singular point)
C = closed curve, traversed once anticlockwise
s287.example: ∮ over |z| = 2 of dz/(z - 1): the point 1 is inside |z| = 2, so the value is 2πi. Around |z| = 2, dz/(z - 3) gives 0, since 3 is outside.

s288.about: For higher powers n ≥ 2, ∮ dz/(z - a)^n = 0 even when a is inside — because 1/(z - a)^n has an antiderivative there (unlike the n = 1 case, which produces the log and the 2πi).
s288.symbols:
n = integer power, n ≥ 2
a = the singular point
s288.example: ∮ over |z| = 1 of dz/z^5 = 0 — only the 1/(z - a) term ever contributes 2πi.

s290.about: Cauchy's formula for derivatives: the n-th derivative at a point inside C is an integral around C — values of f on the boundary determine all derivatives inside. In problems, rearrange the integrand to match f(z)/(z - a)^{n+1} and read off the answer.
s290.symbols:
f^{(n)}(a) = n-th derivative of f at a
n! = n factorial
s290.example: ∮ over |z| = 2 of e^z/(z - 1)^3 dz: here n = 2, f = e^z, a = 1, so the integral = (2πi/2!) f''(1) = πi · e = πei.

s291.about: The Unit 5 problem recipe: (1) factor the denominator and find the singular points; (2) test which lie inside the given curve (|z - a| < radius); (3) points outside contribute nothing; (4) rewrite the integrand with partial fractions so each piece matches Cauchy's formula or the derivative formula; (5) add the contributions. Analytic integrands give 0 immediately.
s291.symbols: |z - a| < r = point a is inside the circle of radius r
s291.example: ∮ over |z| = 2 of dz/(z^2 - 1): poles at ±1, both inside. Partial fractions give (1/2)[1/(z - 1) - 1/(z + 1)], each contributes 2πi, total (1/2)(2πi - 2πi) = 0.
